title: Create stroke/border width tokens in DesignSystem.swift
description:
## Task
Create semantic stroke/border width tokens to replace hardcoded lineWidth values throughout the codebase.

## Why This Matters
Currently border widths are arbitrary:
- `lineWidth: 1` - hairline borders
- `lineWidth: 2` - medium borders  
- `lineWidth: 4` - thick borders (focus states?)

These numeric values have no semantic meaning. A token system provides intent:
- `.hairline` for subtle separators
- `.thin` for card borders
- `.medium` for focus rings
- `.thick` for emphasis

## Implementation

```swift
enum Stroke {
    case hairline  // 0.5pt - subtle separators
    case thin      // 1pt - standard borders
    case medium    // 2pt - focus rings, emphasis
    case thick     // 3pt - strong emphasis
    case heavy     // 4pt - dramatic borders
    
    var width: CGFloat {
        switch self {
        case .hairline: return 0.5
        case .thin: return 1
        case .medium: return 2
        case .thick: return 3
        case .heavy: return 4
        }
    }
}

extension View {
    func stroke(_ stroke: Stroke, color: Color = .border) -> some View {
        self.overlay(
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: CornerRadius.md)
                .stroke(color, lineWidth: stroke.width)
        )
    }
}
```

title: Create overlay opacity scale in DesignSystem.swift
description:
## Task
Create an overlay opacity scale for consistent modal/sheet backgrounds and scrim effects.

## Why This Matters
Overlay opacities are inconsistent:
- LoadingOverlay: `Color.black.opacity(0.3)`
- Some modals: `opacity(0.4)`
- BatchCaptureView gradient: `opacity(0.7)`

Users perceive these inconsistencies as 'cheap.' A systematic scale ensures every overlay feels intentional.

## Implementation

```swift
enum Overlay {
    case subtle    // 0.15 - hint of darkness, content still prominent
    case light     // 0.30 - standard modal scrim
    case medium    // 0.50 - moderate dimming
    case heavy     // 0.70 - strong focus on overlay content
    case opaque    // 0.85 - near-solid, maximum focus
    
    var opacity: Double {
        switch self {
        case .subtle: return 0.15
        case .light: return 0.30
        case .medium: return 0.50
        case .heavy: return 0.70
        case .opaque: return 0.85
        }
    }
}

extension Color {
    static func scrim(_ overlay: Overlay) -> Color {
        Color.black.opacity(overlay.opacity)
    }
}
```

## Use Cases
- `.subtle`: Hover states, subtle dimming
- `.light`: Standard modal backgrounds (most common)
- `.medium`: Photo viewer backgrounds
- `.heavy`: Camera overlays, critical modals
- `.opaque`: Full-screen takeovers

title: Create tiered shadow token system in DesignSystem.swift
description:
## Task
Create a comprehensive 5-tier shadow token system that provides consistent elevation/depth across all components.

## Why This Matters
Currently shadows are hardcoded inconsistently:
- BookCoverCard: `.shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.1), radius: 2, y: 1)`
- BatchCaptureView: `.shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.2), radius: 10, y: 4)`
- glassCard(): `.shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.05), radius: 8, y: 4)`

These arbitrary values create visual inconsistency. A tiered system provides semantic meaning (xs = subtle, xl = floating) that any developer can use consistently.

## Implementation

### Shadow Token Enum
```swift
enum Shadow {
    case xs  // Subtle lift (cards at rest)
    case sm  // Light elevation (hovered cards)
    case md  // Medium depth (modals, popovers)
    case lg  // High elevation (dropdowns, tooltips)
    case xl  // Floating elements (drag preview)
    
    var color: Color {
        switch self {
        case .xs: return Color.black.opacity(0.04)
        case .sm: return Color.black.opacity(0.08)
        case .md: return Color.black.opacity(0.12)
        case .lg: return Color.black.opacity(0.16)
        case .xl: return Color.black.opacity(0.20)
        }
    }
    
    var radius: CGFloat {
        switch self {
        case .xs: return 2
        case .sm: return 4
        case .md: return 8
        case .lg: return 12
        case .xl: return 20
        }
    }
    
    var y: CGFloat {
        switch self {
        case .xs: return 1
        case .sm: return 2
        case .md: return 4
        case .lg: return 8
        case .xl: return 12
        }
    }
}
```

### View Modifier
```swift
extension View {
    func elevation(_ shadow: Shadow) -> some View {
        self.shadow(color: shadow.color, radius: shadow.radius, y: shadow.y)
    }
}
```

### Dark Mode Consideration
Shadow opacity may need slight adjustment in dark mode (less visible). Consider:
```swift
@Environment(\.colorScheme) var colorScheme
// Reduce shadow opacity by 30% in dark mode
```

## Files to Modify
- BookQuotes/Utilities/DesignSystem.swift

## Files to Update After (separate task)
- BookCoverCard.swift
- All places with hardcoded .shadow()

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Shadow enum with 5 tiers defined
- [ ] `.elevation()` view modifier works
- [ ] Shadows look correct in both light and dark mode
- [ ] Documentation comments explain when to use each tier

## Estimated Effort
1-2 hours

title: SUB-EPIC: Foundation - Design Token System
description:
## Overview
Establish a comprehensive design token system in DesignSystem.swift that eliminates all hardcoded visual values and provides a consistent vocabulary for shadows, gradients, strokes, overlays, and advanced animations.

## Why This Matters
Currently, visual values are scattered and inconsistent:
- Shadows: Hardcoded `.shadow(color: .black.opacity(0.05), radius: 8, y: 4)` appears in 5+ places with slight variations
- Gradients: Only 1 LinearGradient in the entire codebase (BatchCaptureView bottom controls)
- Strokes: Hardcoded `lineWidth: 1` or `2` or `4` with no semantic meaning
- Overlays: Inconsistent opacity values (0.3, 0.4, 0.7) for modal backgrounds

Without tokens, every component author invents their own values, leading to visual inconsistency that users perceive as 'unpolished.'

## Current State (DesignSystem.swift)
Already defined:
- Color tokens (brand, accent, semantic)
- Spacing scale (xxs → xxxl)
- Corner radius tokens (sm, md, lg, xl)
- Typography (quoteDisplay, quoteBody, etc.)
- 2 spring animations (smoothSpring, quickSpring)
- 2 transitions (quoteCard, slideUp)

Missing:
- Shadow tokens (tiered depth system)
- Gradient presets (bottomFade, brandGradient, etc.)
- Stroke/border tokens
- Overlay opacity tokens
- Extended animation library
- Motion preferences (Reduce Motion support)

## Deliverables
1. Shadow token system with 5 tiers (xs, sm, md, lg, xl)
2. Gradient presets for common patterns
3. Stroke/border width tokens
4. Overlay opacity scale
5. Extended animation/transition library
6. Reduce Motion utilities
7. iOS 26 Liquid Glass fix

## Technical Considerations
- All tokens should be static constants for performance
- Shadow tokens need both light and dark mode variants
- Animations must check AccessibilityManager for Reduce Motion
- Gradients should use semantic naming (purpose, not appearance)

## Dependencies
- Parent: book-quote-bdo (main UI/UX epic)

## Estimated Effort
8-12 hours

title: Polish EmptyStateView with brand personality and animations
description:
## Task
Transform EmptyStateView from generic and forgettable to branded and delightful, creating a positive first impression for new users.

## Why This Matters
EmptyStateView is what new users see first. It's the app's opportunity to:
- Make a positive first impression
- Communicate brand personality
- Encourage action (add first book)
- Set expectations for the experience

A generic empty state signals 'this is just another app.' A delightful one signals 'this is special.'

## Current State
- Uses `.foregroundStyle(.secondary)` for icon (gray on gray = invisible)
- Generic copy with no personality
- Action buttons are standard `.borderedProminent`
- No animation on appearance
- Three styles exist (default, compact, card) but all feel flat

## Implementation

### 1. Branded Icon with Animation
```swift
// Replace gray icon with brand-colored animated icon
Image(systemName: icon)
    .font(.system(size: 56, weight: .light))
    .foregroundStyle(Color.brand)
    .symbolEffect(.bounce, options: .nonRepeating)  // iOS 17+
    .opacity(appeared ? 1 : 0)
    .scaleEffect(appeared ? 1 : 0.8)
    .animation(.entrance.delay(0.1), value: appeared)
```

### 2. Personality in Copy
```swift
// Context-aware messaging with personality
static func libraryEmpty() -> EmptyStateView {
    EmptyStateView(
        icon: "books.vertical",
        title: "Your library awaits",
        message: "Capture your first book cover to start building your quote collection.",
        actionTitle: "Add Your First Book",
        action: { /* navigation */ }
    )
}

static func searchNoResults(query: String) -> EmptyStateView {
    EmptyStateView(
        icon: "magnifyingglass",
        title: "No matches for '\(query)'",
        message: "Try different keywords or check spelling.",
        actionTitle: nil,
        action: nil
    )
}
```

### 3. Enhanced Action Button
```swift
if let actionTitle, let action {
    Button(action: action) {
        Label(actionTitle, systemImage: "plus.circle.fill")
            .font(.headline)
    }
    .buttonStyle(PrimaryButtonStyle())  // Custom branded style
    .padding(.top, Spacing.md)
    .opacity(appeared ? 1 : 0)
    .offset(y: appeared ? 0 : 10)
    .animation(.entrance.delay(0.3), value: appeared)
}
```

### 4. Card Style Enhancement
```swift
case .card:
    content
        .padding(Spacing.xl)
        .background {
            RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: CornerRadius.lg)
                .fill(LinearGradient.cardHighlight)
        }
        .elevation(.sm)
```

### 5. Staggered Entrance Animation
```swift
@State private var appeared = false

var body: some View {
    VStack(spacing: Spacing.md) {
        iconView
            .animation(.entrance.delay(0.0), value: appeared)
        titleView
            .animation(.entrance.delay(0.1), value: appeared)
        messageView
            .animation(.entrance.delay(0.2), value: appeared)
        actionButton
            .animation(.entrance.delay(0.3), value: appeared)
    }
    .onAppear { appeared = true }
}
```

## Factory Methods for Common Cases
```swift
extension EmptyStateView {
    static var libraryEmpty: EmptyStateView { ... }
    static var quotesEmpty: EmptyStateView { ... }
    static var collectionsEmpty: EmptyStateView { ... }
    static var tagsEmpty: EmptyStateView { ... }
    static func searchEmpty(query: String) -> EmptyStateView { ... }
}
```

## Files to Modify
- BookQuotes/Components/EmptyStateView.swift

- [ ] Brand-colored icon instead of gray
- [ ] Icon has bounce animation on appear
- [ ] Staggered entrance for all elements
- [ ] Context-specific messaging
- [ ] Enhanced action button styling
- [ ] Card style has visual depth
- [ ] Works in dark mode

## Overview
User-defined annotation vocabulary system that personalizes AI extraction. Every reader marks books differently; this feature teaches the AI each user's unique system.

## Background & Rationale
Some readers use single underlines for important passages, double underlines for critical ones, wavy lines for disagreement, asterisks for action items, question marks for research needed. The generic extraction approach misses this semantic richness.

By defining their marking vocabulary, users get:
1. More accurate extraction (AI knows what to look for)
2. Semantic categorization (marking type conveys meaning)
3. Personalized organization (filter quotes by marking type)

## Key Deliverables
1. MarkingDefinition SwiftData model
2. System default markings (underline, highlight, margin line, etc.)
3. Custom marking creation/editing UI
4. Dynamic prompt generation incorporating user's vocabulary
5. Onboarding templates (Academic, Creative, Business, Standard)

- BookQuotes/Features/Settings/MarkingDefinitionEditor.swift
- BookQuotes/Features/Onboarding/MarkingTemplateSelector.swift
- BookQuotes/Services/GeminiService+PromptBuilder.swift

## Technical Considerations
- Visual descriptions must be clear enough for AI to identify in images
- Semantic meanings help with categorization but aren't used in extraction
- Migration path from legacy MarkingType enum to custom definitions
- System defaults can be edited but not deleted
- Sort order matters for prompt construction

title: EPIC: Backend & Subscriptions
description:
## Overview
Lightweight backend infrastructure for API proxying, user authentication, and subscription management. Enables seamless UX without users needing their own API keys.

## Background & Rationale
Consumer apps need frictionless onboarding. Requiring users to obtain API keys, add credit cards to Google, and manage quotas is a non-starter for non-technical users. A simple proxy server with subscription validation solves this.

The economics are favorable: Gemini 2.5 Flash costs ~$0.001 per page extraction. Even heavy users (1000 pages/month) cost ~$1. A $5/month subscription has 80%+ margin.

## Architecture
```
iOS App → Your Proxy Server → Gemini API
              ↓
         Validates:
         - Apple Sign-In JWT
         - Subscription status
         - Usage limits
```

## Key Deliverables
1. Serverless proxy (Cloudflare Workers / Vercel Edge / AWS Lambda)
2. Apple Sign-In authentication
3. StoreKit 2 subscription handling
4. Usage tracking and rate limiting
5. Subscription status sync

## Technical Considerations
- Serverless = near-zero cost at low scale, auto-scales
- Apple Sign-In provides user identity without email/password
- StoreKit 2 server notifications for subscription status
- Could use simple KV storage (no complex database needed)
- Proxy adds ~50-100ms latency (acceptable for this use case)

## Cost Projections
- Cloudflare Workers: Free tier = 100k req/day, $5/mo = 10M req
- Gemini API: ~$0.001/extraction
- 1000 users × 100 extractions/month = $100 Gemini cost
- Revenue at $5/user = $5000/month (50:1 ratio)

## Dependencies
None - this is foundational for the subscription model

1. **Every interaction has feedback** - visual, haptic, or both

description:
## Task
Create a shared ImagePreprocessor/ImageUtilities module that prepares captured images for Gemini requests.

## Why This Matters
Consistent preprocessing improves extraction quality and keeps payload sizes predictable, reducing latency and cost. It should be shared by both cover and quote capture flows.

## Implementation Details
- Normalize orientation (EXIF).

```swift
    }
}
```

title: Implement comprehensive haptic feedback across all interactions
description:
## Task
Audit and implement consistent haptic feedback across all user interactions in the app.

## Why This Matters
Haptics are defined in HapticManager but severely underutilized (only 3 files). Users expect tactile feedback for every interaction - it's a key differentiator of premium iOS apps.

## Current State
HapticManager exists with:
- `light()`, `medium()`, `heavy()` impact
- `success()`, `warning()`, `error()` notification
- `selection()` for UI selection

Only used in:
- BatchCaptureView (capture, error)
- QuoteCaptureView (capture)
- LibraryTab (delete)

## Implementation

### Haptic Guidelines
| Interaction | Haptic Type | Notes |
|-------------|-------------|-------|
| Button tap | light | Every button |
| Primary action | medium | Save, confirm, capture |
| Toggle on | light | Favorite, switch |
| Toggle off | light | Softer than on |
| Selection change | selection | Tabs, filters, pickers |
| Success | success | Save complete, upload done |
| Error | error | Validation fail, network error |
| Warning | warning | Delete, destructive preview |
| Pull refresh | medium | On release |
| Swipe action reveal | light | On threshold |

### Integration Points
1. **All ButtonStyles** - Add haptic to `PressableButtonStyle`
2. **QuoteCardView** - Tap, favorite toggle
3. **BookCoverCard** - Tap
4. **TagChip/FilterPill** - Selection
5. **SearchView** - Scope change
6. **All delete actions** - Warning haptic
7. **Form validation** - Error on invalid
8. **Navigation** - Light on push/pop (subtle)

### Code Pattern
```swift
// In ButtonStyle
.onChange(of: configuration.isPressed) { _, isPressed in
    if isPressed {
        HapticManager.light()
    }
}

// For toggles
.onChange(of: isFavorite) { old, new in
    HapticManager.light()
}

// For actions
func saveQuote() {
    // ... save logic
    HapticManager.success()
}
```

- All ButtonStyles
- QuoteCardView
- BookCoverCard  
- TagChip, FilterPill
- All views with toggles
- All views with destructive actions

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every button has haptic feedback

- [ ] Success/error outcomes have appropriate haptic
- [ ] Haptics feel consistent (not random)
- [ ] Not over-done (some actions can be silent)

description:
## Task
Create reusable gradient presets for common UI patterns like bottom fades, brand gradients, and overlay effects.

## Why This Matters
Currently only 1 gradient exists in the entire codebase (BatchCaptureView bottom controls). Gradients add visual depth and polish:
- Bottom fades make content feel infinite (scrollable lists)
- Brand gradients create visual identity
- Overlay gradients improve text readability on images

Without presets, developers either skip gradients entirely or create inconsistent one-offs.

## Implementation

### Gradient Extension
```swift
extension LinearGradient {
    /// Fade to transparent at bottom - for scroll indicators
    static let bottomFade = LinearGradient(
        colors: [.clear, Color.backgroundPrimary],
        startPoint: .top,
        endPoint: .bottom
    )
    
    /// Dark overlay for text on images
    static let imageTextOverlay = LinearGradient(
        colors: [.clear, Color.black.opacity(0.6)],
        startPoint: .center,
        endPoint: .bottom
    )
    
    /// Brand gradient for premium elements
    static let brandAccent = LinearGradient(
        colors: [Color.brand, Color.accent],
        startPoint: .topLeading,
        endPoint: .bottomTrailing
    )
    
    /// Subtle highlight for cards
    static let cardHighlight = LinearGradient(
        colors: [Color.white.opacity(0.08), .clear],
        startPoint: .top,
        endPoint: .bottom
    )
    
    /// Camera controls overlay
    static let cameraControls = LinearGradient(
        colors: [.clear, Color.black.opacity(0.7)],
        startPoint: .top,
        endPoint: .bottom
    )
}
```

title: Implement cover metadata extraction prompt
description:
## Task
Implement the cover photo analysis prompt and response parsing for book metadata extraction.

## Why This Matters
The prompt engineering determines extraction quality. A well-crafted prompt extracts title, author, publisher, year, and genre from cover photos accurately.

## Implementation Details

### Extraction Prompt
```swift
extension GeminiService {
    func extractBookMetadata(from imageData: Data) async throws -> BookMetadata {
        let prompt = """
        Analyze this book cover image and extract metadata.
        
        Return a JSON object with these fields:
        {
          "title": "The exact book title",
          "author": "Author name(s)",
          "subtitle": "Subtitle if present, or null",
          "publisher": "Publisher name if visible, or null",
          "publishYear": 2023 or null,
          "genre": "Best guess at genre",
          "confidence": 0.95
        }
        
        Rules:
        1. Extract the EXACT title as printed
        2. For multiple authors, use comma separation
        3. Genre should be single category (Fiction, Non-Fiction, etc.)
        4. confidence is 0.0-1.0 for overall extraction quality
        
        Respond with ONLY valid JSON, no markdown.
        """
        
        let response = try await generateContent(prompt: prompt, image: imageData)
        return try parseBookMetadata(from: response)
    }
}

struct BookMetadata: Codable {
    let title: String
    let author: String
    let subtitle: String?
    let publisher: String?
    let publishYear: Int?
    let genre: String?
    let confidence: Double
}
```

title: Implement dynamic quote extraction prompt builder
description:
## Task
Implement dynamic quote extraction prompt that incorporates user's custom marking vocabulary.

## Why This Matters
Each user marks books differently. The prompt must be personalized to look for their specific marking types to achieve accurate extraction.

## Implementation Details

### Dynamic Prompt Builder
```swift
extension GeminiService {
    func buildQuoteExtractionPrompt(markings: [MarkingDefinition]) -> String {
        let enabledMarkings = markings.filter { \$0.isEnabled }
        
        let markingDescriptions = enabledMarkings.map { marking in
            """
            - **\(marking.name)**: \(marking.visualDescription)
              Meaning: \(marking.meaning)
            """
        }.joined(separator: "\n")
        
        let markingTypes = enabledMarkings.map {
            "\"\(\$0.name.lowercased().replacingOccurrences(of: " ", with: "_"))\""
        }.joined(separator: " | ")
        
        return """
        Analyze this book page image to extract marked/highlighted passages.
        
        The reader uses the following marking system:
        
        \(markingDescriptions)
        
        Return a JSON object:
        {
          "quotes": [
            {
              "text": "The exact text that was marked",
              "pageNumber": 42,
              "marginNote": "Any handwritten note near this passage, or null",
              "markingType": \(markingTypes),
              "confidence": 0.92
            }
          ],
          "pageNumber": 42,
          "processingNotes": "Optional notes about extraction quality"
        }
        
        Rules:
        1. Extract COMPLETE marked passage - include full sentences
        2. Match marking type to user's vocabulary above
        3. If multiple marking types, use the primary one
        4. Preserve original formatting where meaningful
        5. Transcribe handwritten margin notes accurately
        6. Include page number if visible
        7. Separate passages = separate quote objects
        8. confidence 0.0-1.0 for each quote's accuracy
        
        Respond with ONLY valid JSON, no markdown.
        """
    }
    
    func extractQuotes(from imageData: Data, markings: [MarkingDefinition]) async throws -> QuoteExtractionResult
}
```

## Task
Build ConfidenceIndicator UI component for visual display of extraction confidence scores.

## Why This Matters
Confidence scores help users identify quotes that may need review. Visual indicators make this information scannable.

## Implementation Details

### ConfidenceIndicator
```swift
struct ConfidenceIndicator: View {
    let confidence: Double
    let style: IndicatorStyle
    
    enum IndicatorStyle {
        case dot, bar, badge
    }
    
    var color: Color {
        switch confidence {
        case 0.9...: return .green
        case 0.7..<0.9: return .yellow
        case 0.5..<0.7: return .orange
        default: return .red
        }
    }
    
    var label: String {
        switch confidence {
        case 0.9...: return "High"
        case 0.7..<0.9: return "Good"
        case 0.5..<0.7: return "Fair"
        default: return "Low"
        }
    }
    
    var body: some View {
        switch style {
        case .dot:
            Circle()
                .fill(color)
                .frame(width: 8, height: 8)
        
        case .bar:
            GeometryReader { geo in
                ZStack(alignment: .leading) {
                    Rectangle()
                        .fill(Color.secondary.opacity(0.2))
                    Rectangle()
                        .fill(color)
                        .frame(width: geo.size.width * confidence)
                }
            }
            .frame(height: 4)
            .clipShape(Capsule())
        
        case .badge:
            Text(label)
                .font(.caption2)
                .padding(.horizontal, 6)
                .padding(.vertical, 2)
                .background(color.opacity(0.2))
                .foregroundStyle(color)
                .clipShape(Capsule())
        }
    }
}
```

### Usage
```swift

HStack {
    Text(quote.text)
    Spacer()
    ConfidenceIndicator(confidence: quote.confidence ?? 1.0, style: .dot)
```

title: Implement QuoteCorrection tracking model
description:
## Task
Implement QuoteCorrection model for tracking user edits to improve future extraction accuracy.

## Why This Matters
User corrections are valuable training signals. Tracking what users change helps identify extraction patterns that need improvement.

## Implementation Details

### QuoteCorrection Model
```swift
@Model
final class QuoteCorrection {
    @Attribute(.unique) var id: UUID
    var quote: Quote
    var originalText: String
    var correctedText: String
    var correctionType: CorrectionType
    var dateCreated: Date
    
    enum CorrectionType: String, Codable {
        case textEdit       // Modified quote text
        case pageNumber     // Changed page number
        case markingType    // Changed marking type
        case marginNote     // Changed margin note
        case deletion       // Deleted incorrect quote
        case addition       // Manually added quote
    }
    
    init(quote: Quote, originalText: String, correctedText: String, type: CorrectionType) {
        self.id = UUID()
        self.quote = quote
        self.originalText = originalText
        self.correctedText = correctedText
        self.correctionType = type
        self.dateCreated = Date()
    }
}
```

### Correction Tracking
```swift
extension Quote {
    func recordCorrection(original: String, corrected: String, type: CorrectionType, context: ModelContext) {
        let correction = QuoteCorrection(
            quote: self,
            originalText: original,
            correctedText: corrected,
            type: type
        )
        context.insert(correction)
        self.dateModified = Date()
    }
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- Model captures before/after state
- Correction type categorizes changes

title: EPIC: Export System
description:
## Overview
Multi-format export enabling users to share their quote collections with external tools: Markdown, Plain Text, JSON, Notion, and Obsidian.

## Background & Rationale
Quote collections gain value when integrated into users' existing workflows. Knowledge workers use Notion; writers use Obsidian; developers want JSON. Local backup ensures data isn't trapped in the app.

Each format has specific requirements:
- Markdown: Human-readable, universally supported
- Plain Text: Simplest, works everywhere
- JSON: Machine-readable, full metadata preserved
- Notion: API-based direct sync with databases
- Obsidian: Markdown files in vault with YAML frontmatter

## Key Deliverables
1. ExportService with format-specific formatters
2. MarkdownFormatter with attribution blocks
3. NotionExporter with API integration
4. ObsidianFormatter with YAML frontmatter
5. Export UI with format selection and preview
6. Local backup to Files app
7. Share sheet integration

## Files
- BookQuotes/Services/ExportService.swift
- BookQuotes/Services/Exporters/MarkdownFormatter.swift
- BookQuotes/Services/Exporters/NotionExporter.swift
- BookQuotes/Services/Exporters/ObsidianFormatter.swift
- BookQuotes/Services/BackupService.swift
- BookQuotes/Features/Export/ExportView.swift
- BookQuotes/Features/Export/ExportPreviewView.swift

## Technical Considerations
- Notion API requires OAuth or integration token; store in Keychain
- Obsidian vault path detection varies by platform
- Large exports should use streaming to avoid memory issues
- Share sheet UIActivityViewController for iOS integration
- Files app export uses UIDocumentPickerViewController

## Acceptance Criteria
- All 5 export formats produce valid, well-formatted output
- User can preview export before executing
- Notion export creates/updates pages in specified database
- Obsidian export generates vault-ready markdown files
- Local backup creates timestamped JSON in Files app
- Share sheet allows sending to any compatible app

## Dependencies
Depends on: EPIC: Project Foundation, EPIC: Library UI (need quotes to export)
